chunks: Typical ground plane layers and why. The question: Which layers typically have ground planes and why?
By convention, ground goes on layer 2, directly under the top signals, and on the layer next to the bottom.
On bigger boards you add more ground planes so that every signal layer has one beside it.
The reason is that a fast signal's return current runs right under it, and a thin gap between the signal layer and a ground plane gives tight return loops and narrow traces.
On a 2-layer board, ground is the bottom layer.
Think of a restaurant where every table must sit next to an aisle so the servers can reach it. A routing layer is a table, and a ground plane is the aisle beside it.
The closer the aisle, the easier the service. The analogy is loose: the plane also shields and stores charge.
The usual ground positions (blue).

Notice the pattern: L2 is always ground; the layer just inside the bottom is ground in boards of four or more layers (except S/G/P/S); each inner signal layer has a ground neighbour; power (orange) sits next to ground.
The 2-layer board is the exception, with only one plane.
Reference plane: the plane next to a signal layer that carries its return current ("Which layers should be ground").
Prepreg: the thin glue layer between outer copper and the first plane ("PCB layers in a stackup and their materials").
Impedance: the ratio of voltage to current a fast signal sees on a trace, in ohms (Ω). It is set by trace width and distance to the plane.
Stripline: an inner trace sandwiched between two planes ("Layers for high-speed signal routing").
Symmetric stackup: layers mirrored around the center so the board stays flat ("Choosing a board stackup").
Compare where the plane sits for a 50 ohms trace, using the page's quick formula (IPC-2141). With ground 0. 2 mm below on layer 2, the trace is 0. 335 mm wide. With the plane 1.
6 mm away on the far side of the board, the same impedance needs about 2. 99 mm, close to 3 mm. A 0. 335 mm trace can squeeze out between the closely spaced pins of a small chip.
A 3 mm trace cannot. That is the whole idea.

"Ground goes on layer 2, directly under the top signals, and on the layer next to the bottom, with more ground planes added so every inner signal layer sits next to one: layers 2 and 5 on six layers, for example.

The reason is return current: outer layers have thin prepreg, so a plane there gives tight return loops and narrow 50 ohm traces; ground beside power adds decoupling capacitance; and inner grounds shield signal layers from each other.
I keep the outer layers for parts and routing, and use stitched pours there."
